prompt.context: Your client is the CEO of Sugar Magnolia Hospital. The hospital is a large, full-service hospital in a large urban area. Over the last five years, the hospital's profitability has decreased to the point that they are almost out of money and will not be able to meet their financial and social mission. The hospital's revenue falls into three categories: (1) Fixed fee for service (e.g., broken leg = $150 to fix), (2) Cost plus (cost of providing the service plus a percentage), (3) Per diem fees (fee per day of hospital stay). The hospital gains patients through physician referral — physicians within the hospital diagnose patients and refer them for care, treatment, surgery, or testing elsewhere in the hospital.
prompt.question: The CEO asks you two things: (1) Why has profitability gone down? (2) How should they turn it around?

clarifying_info.q: Have costs changed significantly recently, e.g. due to a new capital expenditure?
clarifying_info.a: No, there have been no new costs.

clarifying_info.q: Have the prices the hospital charges for services changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: No, prices have not increased or decreased in any considerable way — other than general increases with inflation.

clarifying_info.q: Is the hospital a full-service provider or does it specialize?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital is a full-service provider.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have cost data broken down by patient or patient/service type?
clarifying_info.a: No, we only have aggregate cost data on a per-patient average basis.

clarifying_info.q: What are the key cost figures?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed cost per patient admitted: $1,000. Variable cost per patient per day: $500. Average length of patient stay: 10 days. Patients seen per year: 1,000.

framework: Structure as a profitability problem: Revenues vs. Costs
Revenues = Price x Quantity (number of patients / patient-services). Prices are stable, so focus on volume.
Segment patients/services to identify which segments are growing or declining and why
Costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs per patient per day x average length of stay. Identify levers to reduce cost per patient.
Synthesize: revenue-side (segment mix, referral quality) and cost-side (reducing patient-days) recommendations
Address social mission trade-offs before recommending cost cuts

questions.prompt: What do the four patient/service segments tell you about the revenue decline, and which segments should you prioritize?
questions.guidance: The candidate should note that prices are stable, so the problem lies with volume. There are four segments: (1) Women in Labor/Giving Birth — low profitability, high referral/word-of-mouth, volume DECLINING, fixed fee with high length-of-stay variability; (2) Pediatrics — low profitability, high referral/word-of-mouth, volume DECLINING, fixed fee; (3) Males age 25-50 — medium profitability, medium referral, volume STABLE, per diem and cost-plus rates; (4) Elderly 65+ — high profitability, low referral, volume INCREASING, fixed fee. A strong answer deprioritizes segment 3 (stable), and focuses on segments 1 and 2 because their volume is declining AND they carry high word-of-mouth/referral value that builds long-term patient relationships. The candidate should note that even though elderly are highly profitable, declining word-of-mouth limits long-term growth, and within that segment there may be high-variance long-stay patients driving down profitability.

questions.prompt: How many additional patients could the hospital see if it reduced the average patient stay by 1 day (from 10 to 9 days)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total current patient-day capacity, subtract the new total if stay is reduced by 1 day, then divide the freed capacity by the new average stay length.

math.setup: Current capacity = 1,000 patients x 10 days = 10,000 patient-days. If average stay reduces to 9 days, used capacity = 1,000 x 9 = 9,000 patient-days. Freed capacity = 10,000 - 9,000 = 1,000 patient-days. Additional patients = freed capacity / new average stay.

questions.prompt: How much would total costs decrease if the average patient stay was reduced by 1 day?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current total costs, then recalculate under the reduced-stay scenario, keeping fixed costs constant and reducing variable costs by the saved patient-days.

math.setup: Fixed costs = $1,000 per patient x 1,000 patients. Variable costs = $500 per patient-day x total patient-days. Compare totals before and after the 1-day reduction.
steps: New variable costs (9-day average): 9,000 patient-days x $500 = $4,500,000

brainstorming.prompt: What factors might explain the declining volume in the Women in Labor/Giving Birth and Pediatrics segments, and what actions could reverse the trend?

categories.name: Service quality
ideas: Decline in quality of obstetricians or pediatricians on staff
Poor patient experience scores or reviews

categories.name: Competition
ideas: A competing hospital has begun specializing in obstetrics or pediatrics
A new pediatric urgent-care center has opened nearby
A competitor has invested in a better maternity ward

categories.name: Referral network
ideas: Physicians who previously referred OB/GYN and pediatric patients have left or reduced referrals
Local OB/GYN or pediatric practices have aligned with a different hospital

categories.name: Demographics
ideas: Declining birth rate in the urban catchment area
Population shift away from young families in the area

categories.name: Brand and marketing
ideas: Low visibility in the community for these specialties
Lack of community outreach programs for new mothers or families

recommendation: On the revenue side: invest in the Women in Labor/Giving Birth and Pediatrics segments — they have the highest word-of-mouth and long-term referral potential. Recruit top obstetricians and pediatricians, improve brand in those specialties, and run community outreach.

Further segment the Elderly (65+) cohort to identify high-variance long-stay sub-groups; focus on attracting the profitable, shorter-stay elderly patients while managing the high-variability cases differently.
On the cost side: reducing average patient stay by even 1 day frees ~111 additional patient slots and saves $500,000 in variable costs annually.
risks: Reducing patient-days may conflict with the hospital's social mission to provide quality care; quality-of-care analyses must be completed before any length-of-stay initiative is launched.
If declining OB/GYN and pediatric volumes are driven by physician departures, recruiting replacements takes time and significant investment.
Further segmentation of elderly patients requires detailed data collection and may require additional analytics investment.
next_steps: Conduct research into why OB/GYN and pediatrics volume is declining (exit surveys, physician interviews, competitive landscape analysis).
Perform quality-of-care impact analysis before setting length-of-stay reduction targets.
Build a detailed patient-level cost and revenue database to enable proper segment-level profitability analysis.
Develop a community outreach and physician recruitment plan for target specialties.
